opus-5.5.text:
I wouldn't describe Duplex as AGI, and I don't think anyone who worked on it would have either. What made that demo so striking was that it crossed a threshold in a very specific domain. Calling a restaurant or a hair salon and having a natural back-and-forth, with the disfluencies, the "um"s and "mm-hmm"s, handling interruptions, and the person on the other end not realizing they were talking to a machine, felt like magic at the time. In a sense it was a narrow Turing test that the system passed.

But it was narrow by design. We focused on a handful of tasks, booking appointments, checking business hours, restaurant reservations, because constraining the domain was what made that level of quality achievable back then. The system wasn't reasoning about the world in a general way. It was very good at one kind of conversation, with a lot of careful engineering around understanding, dialogue management, and especially speech synthesis, so it sounded natural and fit the rhythm of a real phone call.

I think the reaction to it says something interesting, though. People tend to equate fluent, humanlike speech with intelligence. When something sounds like a person, we assume there's a person-like mind behind it. Duplex showed how powerful the voice and the conversational dynamics are in shaping that perception. That lesson is even more relevant now, with large language models that are far more general than Duplex was. Today's systems can do things we couldn't imagine in 2018, and even so I'd be careful with the AGI label.

So I'd see Duplex as an early glimpse of what natural human-computer interaction could feel like, not as general intelligence. It was a milestone in making the interaction feel human, which is a different problem from making the system generally intelligent, although the two are converging more and more.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says Duplex should not be described as AGI and explains that it was narrowly designed for specific tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd push back on that framing pretty firmly, honestly. Duplex was never meant to be AGI, and I don't think anyone who worked on it would describe it that way. What we built was a system that was extremely good at a very narrow set of tasks, like booking a restaurant reservation or a haircut appointment over the phone. Within that domain, it could handle a surprising amount of messiness, people talking over it, changing their minds, asking clarifying questions, hold music, all of that. And I think the demo felt impressive because the naturalness of the speech, the "mm-hmm"s and the pauses, made it sound like a person. That's what captured people's imagination.

But sounding human in a two-minute phone call about a dinner reservation is very different from general intelligence. If you tried to take Duplex off script and ask it about, say, the weather or its opinion on a movie, it would fall apart immediately. It had no broad world knowledge, no ability to transfer what it learned about restaurants to some new kind of task without us going in and doing a lot of engineering. Every new vertical required significant effort to build out the dialogue understanding, the state tracking, the recovery strategies. That's the opposite of general.

So I'd say Duplex was a demonstration of what you can achieve when you really constrain a problem and then throw good speech recognition, good synthesis, and a carefully designed dialogue system at it. It was a milestone for conversational AI in the real world, and I'm proud of it. But I think calling it AGI actually does a disservice both to the work, because it sets the wrong expectations, and to the field, because it blurs the line between narrow systems that work well and the much harder problem of broadly capable intelligence. If anything, working on it made me more aware of how far away we were from that at the time.

r001.rationale: The response rejects calling Duplex AGI and describes it as a narrowly capable system, concluding that broad intelligence was still far away.

astra-6.text: I wouldn’t call that artificial general intelligence. It was an impressive demonstration of a system handling a fairly narrow task in a very natural way. And I think that naturalness can make us attribute more intelligence to it than the demonstration actually establishes. Being able to call a restaurant and make a reservation doesn’t tell us whether the same system can handle an entirely different problem. For me, the question is how broadly those capabilities generalize, not just how convincing the system sounds in one conversation.

r001.rationale: The candidate says they wouldn’t call the demonstration artificial general intelligence and describes it as handling a narrow task.

sol-6.1.text: I wouldn’t call it artificial general intelligence. It was an impressive demonstration, but being able to carry out a natural-sounding conversation in a particular setting doesn’t establish general intelligence. Booking an appointment is a fairly constrained task, even if handling the conversation is technically difficult. For me, the question is whether a system can move beyond that setting, adapt to unfamiliar problems, and learn new tasks. The demonstration alone didn’t show that.
